scene_setting.moment: Midday — Babur's tulughma curls around Ibrahim Lodi's wings; Ottoman gunners Ustad Ali and Mustafa light the matchlocks; Lodi dies before nightfall.

synopsis: Foundation moment. Gunpowder + flanking divisions decide north India. Babur's foothold becomes the Mughal Empire.

production_notes.lighting_note: s01 is a DAYTIME OUTDOOR battle — unlike s04 (night interior). Adapt style brief lighting accordingly: midday sun, dusty plains, golden ochre light. Oil lamp references do not apply. Torch/fire can appear at cannon muzzle only.

style_preamble:
[BASE STYLE LOCKED — Round 1 Complete]

Art form:
  Illustrated graphic novel / high-end illustrated narrative.
  Clean, expressive, readable at all scales (thumbnail to full-screen).
  NOT photo-realistic; NOT cartoonish.

Line work:
  Clean ink lines with expressive weight variation.
  Thin for atmosphere, thick for character outlines and emphasis.
  Details (costume, turban gems, facial features) rendered with crisp precision.
  Shadow work (cross-hatching, gradient) creates depth and mood without muddiness.

Color palette (base):
  Primary: Sandstone ochre (architecture, earth), deep burgundy (walls, depth), midnight blue (night sky, far background)
  Accent: Gold (geometric patterns, jewels, highlights), warm amber (oil lamp glow)
  Skin tones: Warm terracotta with amber highlight on lit side, cool shadow on unlit side.
  Palette holds across all panel types.

Character proportions:
  Slightly elongated faces (not cartoonish, but stylized toward expressiveness).
  Accurate historical costume detail (turban shape, jama cut, sash, embroidery).
  Hands rendered with anatomical clarity (gestures legible even when small).
  Beards, turbans, and headgear are visually distinct per character type.

Composition structure:
  Layered like Mughal miniature painting: flat depth (no atmospheric perspective blur).
  Clear foreground / mid-ground / background planes.
  Multiple figures in same scene remain individually legible (no visual clutter).
  Background figures blur appropriately but maintain silhouette clarity.

Lighting model:
  Interior scenes: Warm amber from oil lamps + candelabra. Directional shadows cast dramatically.
  Exterior scenes: Cool moonlight on marble contrasting with warm sandstone.
  Night scenes: Interplay of warm interior glow and cool exterior blue.
  Light source (lamp, window, flame) is always visible and motivates shadow direction.
  Dramatic shadow work on faces in close-ups conveys psychological intensity.

Border/frame convention:
  Thin geometric tessellation border (Mughal geometric motif: interlocking stars, lattice).
  Consistent across all panels.
  Separates panel from surrounding space; reinforces intentional composition feel.

People rule:
  All figures fully illustrated (no raw photographs pasted).
  Historical costume and physical features informed by period sources, but rendered in the unified illustration style.
  Character psychology readable in face and posture at all scales.

[MUGHAL ERA VARIATION]

Color shift:
  Sandstone ochre dominates; jewel tones (deep burgundy, midnight blue) in equal measure.
  Gold used generously (tessellation, jewels, manuscript detail).
  Amber lamplight is the primary night-scene color driver.

Palette:
  Warm: Ochre, amber, terracotta, saffron accent
  Cool: Midnight blue, slate, cool shadow
  Accent: Gold, deep burgundy
  (Result: opulent but controlled; no oversaturation.)

Architectural grammar:
  Red sandstone as primary material (Fatehpur Sikri accurate).
  Persian arches (iwan) as dominant architectural element.
  Jali (lattice) screens visible in windows and decorative panels.
  Geometric carving detail on wall panels, capitals, and ceiling.
  Chahar bagh garden paths implied in exterior scenes.
  Marble domes (Salim Chishti tomb) rendered in cool white/grey.

Lighting (s01 DAYTIME OUTDOOR ADAPTATION):
  Midday sun: harsh, golden, casting short strong shadows on the plain.
  Dust and smoke from artillery: diffuse haze at ground level, backlighting the chaos.
  Late afternoon gold for aftermath/post-battle panels (panels 5, 7).
  No oil lamps in battle panels. Cannon muzzle flash (orange-gold) is the only fire source.

Panel 1 — Establishing (wide battlefield exterior, midday):
The Panipat plain, north India, midday 21 April 1526. Wide composition showing both armies arrayed across a flat, dusty plain with a high horizon line. LEFT side: Babur's Mughal-Timurid cavalry in compact formations — Timurid crescent banners on lances, artillery carts at center with large matchlock cannon mouths visible pointing toward the Lodi line. The tulughma wings of cavalry begin curling outward at the edges of the Mughal formation. RIGHT side: Ibrahim Lodi's army — a mass of war elephant silhouettes (10-12 elephants implied), Lodi infantry in dense ranks, Lodi flags and standards. Between the armies: open dusty ground. The composition reads LEFT versus RIGHT at army scale — no individual figures close enough to identify. Sky: bright midday blue, thinning to dusty haze near the ground. Atmosphere: the held-breath moment before the cannon fires. Art style: illustrated graphic novel, clean expressive ink lines, flat layered depth.

Panel 2 — Wide scene (Babur's field command tent, pre-battle morning):
Babur's open-fronted campaign tent, early morning 21 April 1526. Babur stands at center at a low folding table, in Timurid campaign dress — quilted robe over chainmail at collar, wrapped turban with metal cap, sword at hip. A campaign map of the Panipat region is spread on the table; Babur's finger traces the tulughma flanking arc on the map's left edge. Three military commanders surround him: one points at the map's left flank (the tulughma plan), one holds a runner's folded message, one stands in the tent doorway watching the horizon where Lodi's dust clouds are already rising. Through the tent opening in the background: artillery carts being wheeled into position by turbaned gunners (Ustad Ali's Ottoman crew implied, small scale). Morning light streams golden through the tent opening, illuminating the map and Babur's face. Atmosphere: focused calm, the plan being final-checked before commitment. Art style: illustrated graphic novel, clean ink lines, multiple figures legible, map detail visible but not readable.

Panel 3 — Anchor close-up: Babur, Central Asian conqueror, 43 years old:
Babur on horseback, Panipat battlefield, midday 21 April 1526. Upper-body portrait from the saddle: he wears a quilted Timurid campaign robe (deep burgundy and ochre) with chainmail visible at collar, a firmly wrapped turban with a small metal battle-cap above it. His face: broad, high Central Asian cheekbones, trimmed beard, dark intense eyes — not anger, not fear, but the focused attention of a man who has made the calculation and committed. His right hand rests on the hilt of a curved sword; left hand holds the reins with controlled ease. Behind him over his left shoulder: a Timurid crescent banner on a lance, held by an attendant (partially visible). Background blurred: battlefield dust, cavalry silhouettes, ochre haze. Midday sun from the left warms his face strongly; right side in cooler shadow. Expression: command without swagger — the face of a man who has survived Samarkand twice and knows exactly what he is doing. Art style: illustrated graphic novel, expressive ink work, psychological intensity readable at thumbnail scale.

Panel 4 — Anchor close-up: First Battle of Panipat, 1526 — the decisive moment:
The climactic moment, midday 21 April 1526. FOREGROUND center-left: two Ottoman gunners at a large matchlock cannon mounted on a wheeled cart. Ustad Ali — tall, turbaned, lean and intense — presses a glowing slow-match to the cannon's touchhole with focused deliberateness. Behind him: Mustafa steadies the cannon barrel. The cannon fires: a massive billow of white-grey smoke erupts to the left, the muzzle flash an orange-gold burst. MIDDLE GROUND center-right: the effect on Lodi's line — two war elephants rear in terror at the sound and smoke, trunks raised, their mahouts losing control; one elephant pivots hard into its own Lodi infantry line, causing visible chaos among the foot soldiers. FAR BACKGROUND at frame edges: Mughal tulughma cavalry wings are already curling around both Lodi flanks, encircling the panicked line. The composition is loud and kinetic but legible: cause (cannon) on left, effect (panic) on right, outcome (encirclement) implied at edges. Dust and smoke everywhere, backlit by harsh midday sun. Art style: illustrated graphic novel — dynamic, not cartoonish; the chaos is controlled by composition.

Panel 5 — Anchor close-up (conceptual/symbolic): Mughal Empire — the founding:
Late afternoon, 21 April 1526, somewhere near Panipat or the approach to Delhi. Babur is seated on a portable campaign throne — simple, military, not a palace seat — under a canopied open archway. The plain of north India is visible through the arch behind him, stretching golden in late afternoon light. FOREGROUND: a line of four surviving Lodi amirs and Afghan nobles kneel before the throne, heads bowed, hands joined — submission. One presents the keys of Delhi on a silk cushion extended toward Babur. LEFT of throne: a scribe has begun writing in a large register — the empire's first administrative record, names being inscribed. RIGHT of throne: a standard-bearer holds the Timurid crescent banner upright, now no longer a battle standard but a sovereign flag. Babur's expression: not triumph — the calm of a man who has arrived at a place he calculated for years. The sky through the arch is deep gold verging on amber as the sun drops. Mood: solemnity, not celebration. Art style: illustrated graphic novel — symbolic tableau, the composition more formal and staged than the battle panels, evoking a Mughal court painting's careful arrangement of figures.

Panel 6 — Connective text card: consolidation sequence after Panipat:
At center of the panel, against the deep midnight-blue tessellation background, three short lines of clear, elegant serif text (white or gold):

1527 — Battle of Khanwa: Rana Sanga's Rajput confederacy defeated.
1528 — Battle of Chanderi: Medini Rai's fortress taken.
1529 — Battle of Ghagra: Afghan coalition broken in Bihar.

A thin gold horizontal divider below the three lines, then in slightly larger type:

The foothold becomes territory.

No figures. No map. Pure text-on-tessellation. The tessellation background is ornamental but not overwhelming — fine lines, not solid shapes. The overall effect: a page from a Mughal illustrated manuscript between narrative scenes.

Panel 7 — Fly-by interaction: the Baburnama in the making:
Babur dictates his memoirs — the Baburnama — in a campaign tent or open garden pavilion, a few weeks after the Panipat victory. He reclines on deep burgundy cushions, one hand gesturing mid-sentence (dictating), his expression thoughtful, slightly amused — this is the private Babur, the writer, not the commander. A scribe sits cross-legged before him, quill moving rapidly over an open large manuscript; the manuscript page shows suggested Persian calligraphic script (evocative, not readable). On the low table between them: an ink pot, a second rolled manuscript, a small oil lamp just beginning to be needed as the light changes. Through the tent's open flap or pavilion arch in the background: a newly-planted Chahar Bagh garden — the geometric four-part garden layout Babur laid out after Panipat, the first Timurid garden in north India, visible as young saplings in a formal ochre-path grid, a water channel catching the last afternoon light. Babur brought garden design to India from Kabul; the Baburnama records his grief that India had no proper gardens — this panel shows him making both records at once. Mood: the conqueror as observer, as writer, as man — the intimate register that the Baburnama itself inhabits. Art style: illustrated graphic novel, warm and quiet after the battle's intensity.
